title: Pingiya's devotion (Sn 5)
hook: read it: the old man who can't follow the Buddha on foot but follows him in mind
tomorrow: what do old pages say when you come back to them changed?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mogharaja's question: look on it as empty, mindful, and the king of death doesn't see. And a question to finish the far shore: what if you can't follow your teacher anymore, even on foot?
screen: `LOOK ON IT AS EMPTY.` → `CAN'T FOLLOW, EVEN ON FOOT?`

segments.voice: A video call with a grandparent who can't travel anymore. The screen freezes, the sound lags, and still, somehow, they're right there with you. The way to the far shore ends with a man in that spot. Pingiya, one of the students, is old. He says so himself: weak, his eyes unclear, his hearing poor. He's gone home to his old teacher, Bavari, and someone asks him: why don't you stay with the Buddha?
screen: `A FROZEN VIDEO CALL.` → `PINGIYA IS OLD.` → `WHY DON'T YOU STAY WITH HIM?`

segments.voice: Pingiya's answer, in the closing poem of the way to the far shore, answers yesterday's question: how do you follow someone you can't reach? My body can't go there, he says, but I go there always in thought; my mind is joined to him. I see him with my mind as if with my eye, night and day, watchful, and I spend the night honoring him. So I don't think of myself as apart from him. His faith, joy, mind and mindfulness, he says, don't leave the teaching. That's devotion, Pingiya's way: not travel, but keeping the one you follow in view. Now a neighbor who says something close. In the Hebrew Bible, a psalm read by Jews and Christians alike says, in the King James words: "I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved." What they share: a person who keeps the one they follow before them, always, and finds steadiness in it. The night watch, the right hand; the same human instinct to keep someone near in mind. And the honest difference. The psalmist sets God before him, the LORD at his right hand. Pingiya sets before him a human teacher, honored as awakened, not as God, and his steadiness rests on his own faith and mindfulness staying with the teaching. Two ways of keeping someone close. Neither has to become the other. I follow in mind.
screen: `MY BODY CAN'T GO; MY MIND GOES.` · `I SEE HIM, NIGHT AND DAY.` · `PSALM 16: THE LORD ALWAYS BEFORE ME.` · `SHARED HABIT, DIFFERENT ONE FOLLOWED.` · then, large: `I FOLLOW IN MIND.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable, and bring to mind someone who taught you something good: a grandparent, a coach, a teacher, a friend. See their face as clearly as you can, the way they sat or stood. Rest with them in view, breathing slowly, until the bell.
Pingiya's devotion: an old student who can't follow the Buddha on foot, and sees him with his mind as if with his eye, night and day.
When distance wins the argument: I follow in mind. The way to the far shore, crossed.

howItsDone: Buddhists recollect the Buddha (buddhanussati), bringing his qualities to mind, often before a shrine or image; Pingiya's poem is read as a picture of that practice for someone who can't be near.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 5.18 (Parayananugitigatha, the epilogue: Pingiya to Bavari); Sn 5.17 (Pingiya's question: his age and weak eyes and ears)

sources.quoted: I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved.

notes: Pingiya paraphrased from the Parayanavagga's epilogue (Sn 5.18) and his own question (Sn 5.17: old, weak, eyes not clear, hearing poor). Confirm: Bavari (his teacher) asks why he doesn't stay with Gotama; 'my body cannot go there, but I go always by thought; my mind is joined to him'; 'I see him with my mind as with my eye, night and day, heedful; I spend the night revering him; so I think I am not apart from him'; faith, joy, mind and mindfulness don't leave Gotama's teaching; the Buddha's closing words to release faith (as Vakkali, Bhadravudha and Alavi-Gotama did).

Unity thread (wisdom shape): shared with the Hebrew Bible's Psalm 16:8 (KJV, quoted), read by Jews and Christians: keeping the one followed always before you, steadied by it. Honest difference: the psalmist sets God (the LORD) before him; Pingiya sets a human teacher honored as awakened, not as God, and his steadiness rests on his own faith and mindfulness. No ranking. Please confirm both are described fairly (Jewish and Christian readers both).
'Honored as awakened, not as God' is a general statement of Buddhist understanding; confirm phrasing with the Keeper.
Gloss 'LORD': KJV small capitals render the Tetragrammaton; confirm the short gloss.
